title: The Turtle That Never Forgets the Way Home

blocks.prompt: The Turtle That Never Forgets the Way Home
blocks.text: A green sea turtle spends almost all of its life in the ocean. It flaps its long front flippers and flies through the water. But every mother turtle has one job on land. She crawls up a beach at night. She digs a deep hole in the sand with her back flippers. She lays her eggs. Then she covers them up and goes back to the sea. The eggs sit warm in the sand for about two months. One night the babies dig their way out. They run down the sand and swim away. Here is the strange part. That mother turtle hatched on that same beach, years and years ago.

blocks.prompt: The Longest Run of Their Lives
blocks.text: A green sea turtle egg is soft and round, about the size of a ping pong ball. The mother buries about a hundred of them in the warm sand and then leaves. She never comes back. Nobody guards the nest. About two months later, the hatchlings break out of their shells. They dig upward together, a whole nest of them pushing the sand down under their feet. They wait just below the surface until the sand feels cool. Cool sand means the sun has gone down, and the dark is safer. Then the run begins. The hatchlings scramble across the beach toward the brightest thing they can see. On a wild beach, that bright thing is the open sky above the water. Crabs and gulls are waiting. Most hatchlings never make it. The ones that reach the waves keep swimming for days without stopping. Out of every thousand hatchlings, only about one will live long enough to grow up.

notes: Named for its green fat, not its shell

blocks.prompt: The Lost Years
blocks.text: For a long time, scientists could follow the life of a green sea turtle only at its two ends. They could watch the hatchlings sprint down the beach. They could watch the grown females crawl back up it decades later. In between there was nothing. The little turtles swam out past the surf and simply vanished. Researchers gave that gap a name: the lost years. We now know roughly where they go. Currents carry the hatchlings out into the open ocean, where they shelter in drifting mats of sargassum, a floating seaweed that gathers into long golden lines on the surface. Tucked into that tangle, a young turtle finds food and cover far from the beaches where everything wanted to eat it. It stays out there for years. When a green turtle finally returns to shallow water, it changes its diet completely. Young ones eat almost anything they find: jellyfish, crabs, small drifting animals. Adults become vegetarians. They spend their days cropping seagrass and scraping algae off rocks, and their bodies fill with green fat from all those plants. That fat is where the name comes from. Their shells are not really green at all. The grazing matters more than it sounds. A seagrass meadow that is never cropped grows long, mats over, and rots from underneath. Turtles mow it, and the meadow stays healthy, which keeps the fish and shrimp that live in it alive too. Take out the turtles and the meadow can go with them.

(inference: uncropped seagrass mats over and rots, so grazing keeps the meadow and its fish alive)

notes: Chelonia mydas
Natal homing: back to their own hatching beach

blocks.prompt: The Map They Are Born With
blocks.text: A female green sea turtle may spend thirty years and several thousand miles away from the beach where she hatched. Then, one season, she turns around and swims back to it. Not to that stretch of coast in general. To that beach. Turtles marked as hatchlings have been found nesting within a few miles of the sand they crawled out of, decades later. Biologists call this natal homing, and for most of the last century nobody could explain it. The leading answer is magnetism. The Earth is wrapped in a magnetic field, and that field is not identical everywhere. Its angle and its strength shift gradually as you move north or south along a coastline, so each stretch of beach sits under a slightly different magnetic signature. The current explanation is that a hatchling records the signature of its home beach during those first frantic minutes in the water, files it away, and carries that number around for the rest of its life. The evidence is strong. Researchers have placed young sea turtles in tanks ringed with coils that can imitate the magnetic field of a faraway location. Feed a turtle the field of a spot north of its range and it swims south. Feed it the field of a spot to the south and it turns north. It has never been to either place. It is correcting course on a map it was born holding. There is a stranger piece still. Along real coastlines, nesting beaches with similar magnetic signatures tend to host genetically similar turtles, even when those beaches are far apart. The turtles are not sorting themselves by distance. They are sorting themselves by field. None of this makes them safe. A turtle can navigate an entire ocean and still arrive at a beach that is now a parking lot, a seawall, or a row of lights bright enough to send her hatchlings running the wrong way. The map in her head is older than the buildings on the shore, and nobody has updated it.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Turtle That Never Forgets the Way Home

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Chelonia mydas
The sea turtle line is over 100 million years old
Sand temperature decides male or female
No sex chromosomes at all
Adults can top 300 pounds
Turtle excluder devices cut deaths in nets
Hawaii and Florida nesting numbers have climbed

blocks.prompt: The Temperature of the Sand
blocks.text: Sea turtles have been doing this for a very long time. Their lineage was swimming and nesting before the extinction that ended the dinosaurs, and it came through that event intact. The animal hauling itself up a beach tonight is running a program that has already survived an asteroid. It is worth knowing what that program depends on. Start with the shell. A land tortoise, threatened, pulls its head and legs inside and waits it out. A sea turtle cannot. Its shell is flattened into a wing shape and its limbs have stretched into paddles, and there is simply nowhere for the head to go. Speed and size replaced armor. An adult green turtle can weigh over three hundred pounds and drives itself forward with its front flippers in a motion that looks much less like swimming than like flying. The trade was straightforward: the ocean got easier, and hiding became impossible. Then the eggs. A green sea turtle has no sex chromosomes deciding whether a hatchling becomes male or female. The sand decides. Eggs incubating in cooler sand, below roughly 82 degrees Fahrenheit, produce mostly males. Warmer sand, above about 88 degrees, produces mostly females. Between those numbers sits a narrow band that yields a mix. The entire system is balanced on a few degrees of beach. For a hundred million years that was a reasonable bet. Beaches varied, some nests sat in shade and some in sun, and the numbers averaged out across a season. It is a worse bet now. On some heavily studied nesting grounds, surveys of young green turtles have come back over ninety percent female. A population can absorb that for a while, because one male will mate with several females. It cannot absorb it forever. A species does not need to be hunted to disappear. It only needs to stop producing males. The rest of the pressure is more ordinary. Hatchlings find the water by running toward the brightest horizon, a rule that worked flawlessly until people lit the land. Now the brightest horizon is often a road. Adults mistake plastic bags for jellyfish. Nesting beaches become hotels. Fishing nets drown air-breathing animals that cannot reach the surface. And yet the honest ending is not despair, because this is one of the few conservation stories where the fixes demonstrably work. Escape hatches built into trawl nets, called turtle excluder devices, let a caught turtle push its way out. Protected beaches, shielded streetlights, and shaded nests raise the number of hatchlings that reach the water. Green turtle nesting has climbed substantially at major sites in Hawaii and Florida since protections began. Slow animals respond slowly, and decades passed before those graphs turned upward, which is exactly why this work is hard to fund and easy to abandon. The turtle carries a magnetic map, a shell built for the open ocean, and a hundred million years of successful practice. What it does not carry is any way to notice that the sand got warmer. That part is our job.
